title: Ratthapala's fast
hookLine: a young man fasts until his parents let him ordain; years later they try to tempt him home

lines: HE LIES DOWN ON THE BARE FLOOR.
cards: Raṭṭhapāla is the only son of a wealthy family in a town in the Kuru country. He hears the Buddha teach once, and he knows: he wants to go forth, to become a monk.
The Buddha says he can't ordain anyone without their parents' consent. So Raṭṭhapāla goes home and asks. They say no.
He's their only child, dear to them, raised in comfort. He asks again. No.
So he lies down on the bare floor and says: I will either die right here, or go forth.

teach.b: He doesn't eat. One meal, two, three, up to seven, the sutta says. His parents beg.
His friends beg: get up, eat, enjoy your life, you can do good as a householder. He says nothing. Finally the friends go to the parents: if you refuse, he'll die.
If you let him go, at least you'll see him alive.

teach.h: YOU MUST COME BACK TO VISIT.
teach.b: They agree, on one condition: after he's ordained, he must come back to visit. Later, he does, walking for alms in his own hometown.
His father, having his hair dressed in the hall, sees a shaven-headed monk at the door and doesn't recognize his own son.
He mutters against the monks who took his only child, and Raṭṭhapāla gets nothing, not even a polite refusal. On his way out, a family servant is about to throw away yesterday's porridge.
He asks her to put it in his bowl, and as she does, she knows him, by his hands, his feet, his voice. She runs to his mother.
The next day his father piles up gold and silver in the house. Take this, he says. Come home.
Enjoy your wealth and do good. Raṭṭhapāla's former wives are dressed in their finest. He answers his father calmly: put it all on carts, and sink it in the Ganges.
It will only bring you grief.
He stood by it. Not by shouting, or by cutting his family off, but by coming back exactly as he'd promised, eating their old porridge, and saying no kindly. The fast was the drama.

how: In Theravada practice a candidate for ordination is asked whether their parents consent, and monks may return to visit family; in some countries young men ordain for a short time partly to honor their parents.

o: an only son's refusal to eat until his parents consented
a fast monks keep each year before their ordination
a father's fast to bring his monk son back home

p: lay on the floor, didn't eat
knew him by his hands, feet, voice
piled gold to tempt him home

s: Raṭṭhapāla ran away from home to become a monk
the Buddha required his parents' consent, and he waited for it.
his father didn't recognize him at first
he saw a shaven-headed monk at the door and didn't know his own son.
the parents agreed on condition that he come back to visit
and later he kept the promise.

games.q: you're Raṭṭhapāla, home as a monk. your father has piled up gold and silver. 'take it. come home.' what does the text say you answer?
o: take a little, for the monastery
load it on carts and sink it in the Ganges
games.why: he tells his father, calmly, that the wealth will only bring grief, and refuses it, without leaving in anger.

practice: Think of a choice you've made that someone you love doesn't like, a job, a move, a belief, and picture their face. Notice any urge to defend yourself loudly, or to give in.
Then picture a third way, staying with your choice and staying warm toward them, the way Raṭṭhapāla came home and ate the porridge.

wordCard.voice: Raṭṭhapāla's fast. An only son lies on the floor until his parents let him go forth, and later comes home as he promised, and kindly says no to their gold.

orig.note: Pali pabbajjā: going forth, leaving home for the homeless life. what Raṭṭhapāla fasted for.

carryVoice: Your line: he stood by it. Kindly, calmly, and with the promise to visit kept. Until tomorrow.
